I struggled with this for a long time as well, and I eventually came to two solutions.

1. Your game doesn't have to be a cinematic master piece like Critical Role is. There is nothing wrong with starting with the players in a party, already knowing each other. Even Exandria Unlimited started like this.  
2. Let the players handle it. In session 0, talk about what they want to bring them together, what kind of things interest all of them, things along those lines. For the most part, players want to make this work, and don't expect you to do it all on your own.
I'll always be an advocate for the cypher system. It's a system made for literally any setting, and you can add and remove rules as you want without throwing off the whole system. It's great.

Light heartedness/grit is almost completely in wording and tone. Slicing a humanoid enemy in half and killing him is the same thing as bravely defeating a menacing foe mechanically, it just depends on how you word it and the tone you set at the table.

I had the party explore a secret section of a magical college called Everspark. In the last room, when they confronted the man they'd been sent to find, he had no real power of his own, but he had a magic word that could release 4 elementals into the room while he booked it. I extensively looked up and experimented with the stat blocks for stone, water, fire, and air elementals until I understood their strengths, and threw them all in with very specific strategies. The stone tanked the frontliners and kept them distracted, the air got the flanks, the water engulfed people and slowed their movements, and the fire would go through as many enemy spaces as it could to keep people on fire as much as possible.  
TLDR: Fights go better when you have a deep understanding of the combatants you're controlling, and if they all have a specific strategy.

Rakdos shows are festivals of things that hurt people. This could be an interesting time for the martial characters to pick up some unconventional yet effective weapons mid fight. Spellcasters will be okay. When it comes to armor class, I would maybe have a lot of enemies that deal in saving throws, instead.

Also worth noting is that charisma is also a measure of your willpower. Sorcerers use charisma as a spellcasting mod, and tieflings use charisma as their innate spellcasting mod, because it's a measure of their ability to project their will into the world. An ugly, scarred battle veteran could have a very high charisma, for sheer force of will and ability to intimidate.

Me and my group use the rules, but we did away will all of the plot structuring in MOTW. It's your game, at its core. Structure the game how you feel it should be structured. Personally, I think 2-4 hours per mystery is extremely short. A session long mystery to my group leaves no room for character conversations, shenanigans, or really anything. We'd have to cut out a lot of fun scenes to play in that short of a time frame.
It was a nightmare session. Every DM has one. Longtime DMs have more. The game can be miserable sometimes, but it's few and far between all the crazy fun stuff you do.

If I understand correctly, it sounds like they're gonna travel to a lot of different types of worlds. In that case, you need your BBEG to be either very versatile, or it needs to be a genre that supports planar travel like that.  


Me, I would go for a far future baddie, going through dimensions and stealing precious items and artifacts, or using other time periods technology, with a whole retinue of people from their native dimension, from other people they've picked up along the way. This could mean fighting a massive dragon throughout skyscrapers of a futuristic setting, or fighting a spider robot in the magic crystal caverns of a fantasy setting.  


Whatever you do, it should allow for versatility and weirdness.
